kicker: Telning Publishing House · The TADA way
lead: Our own way to turn a picture book into a real talk with your child.
intro: TADA is Telning's own way to talk about a story. You talk with your child, you ask, your child decides how the story ends, and then you act: you take the story into real life. It works with every Telning book, in any language you speak at home.
byline: By the Telning team of cognitive and behavioural scientists

built.text: TADA is our own way to talk about a story. Our cognitive and behavioural scientists built it after a careful review of the research, including meta-analyses and trials on shared reading, wordless books and talking about feelings

steps.t: Meta-analyses and trials on shared reading, wordless books and talking about feelings.

steps.h: We added what we learned in our work
steps.t: What we see when we work with children and families, week after week.

steps.h: We made it four easy steps for home
steps.t: Talk, Ask, Decide, Act. Short enough to remember at bedtime.

science.lead: Five findings in plain words. Each card links to its source at the bottom of the page.
science.dialogicText: Dialogic reading is a way of sharing a book where the child does more of the talking. The grown-up asks a question, listens, repeats the child's words and adds one or two. Over time the child becomes the storyteller. TADA is built on it.

cards.t: Children who talked about feelings after a story understood feelings better than children who heard the same stories without that talk.

cards.h: Talking with a child helps more than reading to a child.
cards.t: Large reviews of dialogic reading agree.
With wordless books, parents ask more open questions and children say more.
Young children learned more words when one picture was shown at a time. That is why our books have one picture per sheet.
Busy, decorated rooms pulled young children's attention away. So our pages stay simple.

items.h: Decide is a step of its own.
items.t: The story stops at a fork: two endings, side by side. Your child chooses and says why. There is no wrong answer.
The grown-up asks, waits, and adds one word.

items.h: Act takes the story into real life.
items.t: "What would you do?" Then your child draws their own ending.
You send the drawing. We send a story card and ideas for your next talk.

items.h: Wordless, so it works in any language.
items.t: The story belongs to you and your child, in the language you speak at home.
Your child sees the choices, thinks about what could happen, picks one and says why. Feelings, friends and new ways to act are woven in.

steps.h2: How do the four steps work?
steps.lead: Who does what, three things you can say, and one tip for a two-year-old and one for a six-year-old.

list.name: Talk
list.what: Your child looks at the page and says what they see. You wait. Then you repeat their words and add one or two.
list.young: Point and name things together. You do more of the talking, and that is fine.
list.older: Let your child tell the whole page before you say anything.

list.name: Ask
list.what: One easy question first: who, what, where. Then one about feelings or why.
list.young: One question per page. Count to five in your head before you help.
list.older: Ask "What could happen next?" before you turn the page.

list.name: Decide
list.what: At the fork, two endings sit side by side. Your child picks one and says why. There is no wrong answer.
list.young: Your child points. You can colour that ending together.
list.older: Ask what each ending would change for the others in the story.

list.name: Act
list.what: Take the story into real life. Then your child draws their own ending, and you send it to Pim.
list.young: Act it out with a toy. Keep it short.
list.older: Let your child draw the ending alone, then tell you the story of it.

honest.h2: What research shows, and what it does not show yet
honest.p1: Effects of shared reading are small to medium, and they fade without practice. So: short sessions, often, and read the same book again.
honest.p2: No study has tested choose-your-ending picture books yet. We use the fork to start a talk, and we are testing it with families.
